description: Proyecto orientado a desarrollo de software espacial y estudio de datos.
summary:
We developed OrbitalUV, an interactive web tool that recommends landing sites near the Moon’s south pole for dates selected by the user. The tool addresses a challenge for Artemis missions: finding sites where sunlight is available for solar power while Earth is visible for direct communication.

Using NASA’s LOLA elevation data and planetary ephemerides, OrbitalUV calculates the local horizon at 315 candidate sites and checks when the Sun and Earth are both above it. The tool runs these calculations directly in the browser and recommends up to six zones, each with a primary site and backup options. Interactive maps, charts, and a light and shadow simulation show how the terrain affects both conditions.

A site that looks promising on a long-term illumination map may offer limited sunlight or lose sight of Earth during a specific mission window. By letting users compare sites and dates, OrbitalUV supports early mission planning and helps students and the public understand the trade-offs behind choosing a lunar landing site.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

OrbitalUV is an interactive website that recommends where to land near the Moon’s south pole for any dates the user selects between 2025 and 2040. It identifies sites with the most time when both sunlight is available for power generation and Earth is visible for direct communication.

It works in three steps.

  1. Using NASA’s LOLA laser altimetry data, with one elevation measurement every 80 m, we calculate the local horizon at each site. We determine how high the surrounding terrain blocks the sky in each direction, looking up to 150 km away and accounting for the Moon’s curvature.
  2. Using NASA’s official NAIF DE440 ephemerides, we calculate the positions of the Sun and Earth over time. Our calculated positions agree with JPL Horizons to within 0.001°.
  3. Every few minutes throughout the selected period, the browser checks whether both the Sun and Earth are above the local horizon at each of the 315 candidate sites. It then groups the sites into up to six recommended zones, each with a primary site and several backups.

OrbitalUV also provides maps of sunlight and Earth visibility for any selected period, a light and shadow simulation, charts showing the elevation of the Sun and Earth relative to the local horizon, and landing windows for each site.

What are the benefits?

  • Specific recommendations. OrbitalUV shows where to land on the selected dates, going beyond multi-year averages.
  • Accessibility. It runs in any browser without installation, server-side computation, or prior knowledge of astronomy.
  • Transparency. It uses official NASA data, cites its sources, and clearly identifies which figures come from NASA and which are calculated by OrbitalUV.
  • Validation. Compared with NASA’s official PGDA 69 maps, our maps differ by an average of 1.4 percentage points for illumination and 2.7 percentage points for Earth visibility, with a correlation of 0.98.

What is the expected impact?

OrbitalUV helps students, science communicators, and space enthusiasts explore one of the Artemis programme’s key decisions: where to land near the lunar south pole. It can also support early mission planning by helping users assess candidate landing sites, compare dates, and understand how strongly terrain affects sunlight and direct communication with Earth. The method could be extended with higher-resolution terrain maps to identify rocks and assess slopes at the scale of a lunar lander.

What tools, languages, hardware, and software did we use?

  • Data. NASA’s LOLA terrain data (PGDA 90), PGDA 69 illumination maps, NAIF DE440 ephemerides, JPL Horizons tables, and official International Astronomical Union (IAU) names.
  • Data preparation. Python with NumPy, Numba, Rasterio, SpiceyPy (for NASA’s SPICE toolkit), Pandas, Pillow, and pytest.
  • Website and browser-based calculations. JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and Web Workers, with Plotly.js for charts.
  • Version control and hosting. Git and GitHub for the code, and Firebase Hosting (Google Cloud) for deployment.
  • Hardware. Our personal laptops.

What makes it creative?

  • Calculations for your exact dates. OrbitalUV goes beyond an 18-year average by performing minute-by-minute calculations directly in the browser.
  • Power and communication in one criterion. It looks for periods when sunlight is available and Earth is visible at the same time, and always provides backup sites.
  • Complex data made visual. It turns terrain models, ephemerides, and local horizons into maps, charts, and a simulation that anyone can explore.

What factors did we consider?

  • Science. Sunlight, Earth visibility (even part of Earth’s disc above the horizon counts), lunar terrain and curvature, a maximum slope of 10°, locations south of 84° S (the Artemis III area), long lunar nights, and interruptions to direct communication.
  • Scientific rigour. Official NASA datasets, validation against official maps, and automated tests.
  • Stated limitations. The 80 m terrain data cannot resolve rocks or small craters. The results describe geometric visibility only. Actual power generation, a reliable radio link, and a safe landing require further assessment.
  • User experience. A bilingual website in Spanish and English, with light and dark themes, a mobile-friendly layout, and offline functionality.
